explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion. It cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) Picture shoving a mountain. You'd pull a muscle before it budged an inch, and I'd be the guy cheering from the sidelines, waving my mustache like a flag.

I get why a mountain makes you think "biggest." But the psalm never talks about height. It says Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) The point is staying put, not winning a tallest-peak contest.

Green is a nice guess, friend, but the psalm doesn't mention it. What it says about Mount Zion is, "It cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) That's what the picture is about: steady, no matter what.

Careful, friend, this one's flipped. The psalm says the opposite: Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) A season is about how long a plate of my cookies lasts once the bakery door opens. Forever is a whole other category.
Right, baker. The psalm says Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) Forever and a season are not even in the same bakery. Nobody ever called a mountain a limited-time offer.

Yes! "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) Think of the mountains standing all the way around the city. That's the picture of how the LORD surrounds them. I'd say that's a pretty great place to be standing.

Priests are a fair guess, baker, but they aren't in this verse. It says, "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) His people, all of them. Nobody's left out of that circle.

I see why you'd pick king, but the psalm doesn't say that here. The verse reads, "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people…" (Psalm 125:2) His people is the whole crowd, friend, not one name on the list.

That's it, baker. The psalm says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) No expiration date stamped on the box. Nothing to check, nothing to toss when the date runs out.
That sounds sensible, friend, but the psalm doesn't put any condition on it. It says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) No "until," just now and forevermore.

explanations.answer: As long as the city stands
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the psalm doesn't tie it to the city. It says the LORD surrounds His people "…both now and forevermore." (Psalm 125:2) The mountains are the picture. The forevermore is what the verse says.

explanations.answer: So the righteous won't turn to injustice
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says the scepter of the wicked will not rest on the land, "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) That "so that" is the reason, plain as flour on my apron.

explanations.answer: So the righteous can grow their harvest
explanations.explanation: Harvest is a nice thought, but this verse doesn't mention one. It gives its reason right there: "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) That's the "why" the psalm gives.

explanations.answer: So the wicked will turn and repent
explanations.explanation: Harder to guess a reason than it looks, friend, and that one isn't in the verse. The reason it gives is "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) Nothing about the wicked turning in this verse.

That's right. The psalm prays, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) Short and simple. That prayer doesn't need a long wind-up, and I admire that, because I once gave a speech about one cookie and ran out of oven time.

Long life sounds lovely, baker, but it's not what the psalm asks here. The prayer is, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) The ask is simply for the LORD to do good.

Great names, ha! Nice guess, friend, but that's not in this verse. The psalm says, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4) The request is for the LORD to do good to them.

Yes, baker. The psalm says, "But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers." (Psalm 125:5) It's a serious line, so I'll just say it plainly. It sits right next to the prayer for the upright in heart.

Not this time, friend. The psalm does say it: "But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers." (Psalm 125:5) I think it's a heavy line, and the psalm doesn't soften it. It's also followed right away by "Peace be upon Israel."
